The addition of **“Lumbar spine MRI (without contrast), with dedicated axial T2-weighted sequences at L4–L5”** — explicitly ordered *to assess disc herniation morphology, size, and degree of L5 nerve root compression* — is clinically precise and appropriate. This refined summary reinforces the diagnosis of acute L5 radiculopathy with high clinical fidelity. The key insight is the distinction between *radicular pain* (driven by inflammatory/chemical irritation of the nerve root) and *radiculopathy* (defined by objective neurological deficit). Here, the patient has unequivocal radicular pain in the L5 distribution and a highly positive SLR—both strongly predictive of underlying disc pathology—but preserved motor and sensory function confirms the root is irritated, not significantly compressed or dysfunctional. This “neurologically intact radiculopathy” is typical of early or mild disc herniations (e.g., small contained protrusions at L4–L5), where cytokine-mediated inflammation and mechanical stretch—not axonal compromise—drive symptoms. Acute L5 radiculopathy secondary to a small or contained L4–L5 intervertebral disc herniation
